query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing local chemical ordering through modified annealing treatments shifts the phase balance in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys toward a higher fraction of ordered B2 domains, thereby tuning phase stability to achieve improved high‐temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized or moderately annealed multiphase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA exhibiting a mixed state of ordered (B2) and disordered (FCC/BCC) phases with moderate local chemical order.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment with increased duration or temperature (while keeping global composition constant) to systematically enhance the degree of local chemical ordering.
generation.conditions: Comparison of two sets of identical alloy samples: one subjected to a baseline (moderate) annealing regime and the other to an enhanced annealing regime. Experiments are conducted across service-relevant conditions ranging from cryogenic to high temperatures to simulate environmental, radiation, and mechanical stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local chemical (short-range) ordering that promotes the nucleation and growth of the ordered B2 phase over the disordered FCC/BCC phases.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced local chemical ordering reduces the effective formation energy of the B2 phase via stronger, composition-specific atomic interactions (influenced by mixing enthalpy and atomic size mismatch). This results in a shift in phase fractions and transformation temperatures, thereby directly linking microstructural ordering to multi-environment mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples in the enhanced annealing condition will display a higher B2 phase fraction and altered transformation temperatures compared to the baseline. This shift is expected to correlate with increased high-temperature strength and radiation tolerance, alongside optimized cryogenic toughness. However, if the ordering becomes excessive, a trade-off may occur, leading to embrittlement.
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy annealed under moderate conditions resulting in a balanced mixture of ordered and disordered phases with average performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within an annealing regime where local chemical ordering is tunable—specifically, for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni compositions near the critical threshold between single-phase and multiphase behavior. It is limited to processing conditions that are neither so mild as to prevent meaningful ordering nor so extreme as to induce uncontrollable embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of phase fraction shifts and the precise transformation temperature changes remain uncertain, as they depend on processing nuances and the sensitive interplay of local ordering effects with macroscopic performance. Further calibration is required to establish optimal annealing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples. Subject one set to a baseline annealing treatment (moderate temperature/time) and the other set to an enhanced annealing treatment (increased temperature and/or duration) designed to increase local chemical ordering. Characterize microstructure using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify phase fractions and local order. Additionally, measure phase transformation temperatures and assess mechanical properties under high-temperature, radiation, and cryogenic conditions.
measurements: Phase fractions of ordered (B2) versus disordered (FCC/BCC) phases via XRD/TEM
Mechanical properties such as high-temperature strength, cryogenic toughness, and radiation tolerance indicators
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced annealing treatment does not yield a significant increase in local chemical ordering (as evidenced by unchanged or similar phase fractions and transformation temperatures) or if any microstructural changes observed do not correlate with improvements in high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, or cryogenic toughness compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. Abstract Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. Here, an unexpected ductile–brittle–ductile transition is discovered in a multiphase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) aged in an intermediate temperature regime. Unlike the classical thermal embrittlement driven by grain boundary effects, this transition originates from the dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations in HEAs. Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition. In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery. The findings offer new insights into the thermal behavior of HEAs and challenge the established paradigm of thermal embrittlement. The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [7] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ] This well‐established mechanism highlights the central role of brittle phase precipitation and element segregation at GBs in governing embrittlement in conventional alloys.

In contrast, emerging high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), [ [15] , [16] , [17] ] which consist of multiple principal elements, introduce new thermodynamic and kinetic complexities that challenge conventional thermal exposure paradigms. Their high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion kinetics [ [

In summary, our study deciphers an unusual ductile−brittle−ductile transition in a eutectic HEA, driven by the dynamic evolution of LCOs and PBs configurations. Enhanced LCOs and the formation of jagged PBs lead to brittleness, while controlling the order degree of LCOs and the formation of a ductile transition zone along the PBs recovers the ductility. This discovery highlights the critical role of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and PBs in determining material behavior, challenging and expanding the traditional paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Although LCOs are generally beneficial for strength‐ductility synergy in HEAs, our findings reveal their dual role: excessive ordering induces brittleness, whereas controlled LCOs restore ductility, which further indicates the necessity of meticulous control of LCOs for better performance. We believe that the uncover of thermal evolution behavior of HEA will advance the high‐temperature application of the HEA family.

This trend is particularly important for multi-component alloys, because the ordering can drive the system to various microstructural states, such as crystalline or intermetallic solids, from the disordered FCC ( A1 ), BCC ( A2 ), or HCP ( A3 ) conditions. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

frame.system: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys in their as-synthesized (or annealed) multiphase state, where phase formation includes both ordered and disordered arrangements (e.g., potential B2-ordered and FCC/BCC disordered phases)
frame.goal: To develop a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains how phase stability is controlled in these alloys and how that stability underpins the simultaneous retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
frame.limitation: There is currently no unifying, mechanistic understanding that links the complex interplay of composition-driven atomic interaction (including local chemical order, atomic size mismatch, and mixing enthalpy) with the formation and stability of phases that deliver the combined performance properties.
root_cause_cues: retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness
constraints: Must specify a controlled comparison (for example, comparing a modified alloy with altered atomic-size mismatch or local order to a baseline composition)
Must predict observations relative to a baseline (e.g., differences in phase fractions or transformation temperatures)
Define the boundaries of the hypothesis (i.e., the regime where local chemical ordering or lattice distortion effects dominate)
Incorporate supporting prior evidence (such as earlier studies linking mixing enthalpy and atomic size mismatch with phase evolution)

Identify a specific observation that would falsify the hypothesis (for instance, if the controlled change in local ordering does not lead to the predicted shift in phase boundaries or mechanical performance)
frame.regime: The hypothesis applies across a range of conditions encompassing high-temperature operating conditions, radiation exposure regimes, environmental attack conditions, and cryogenic temperatures, reflecting the multi-environmental challenge faced in application.
prior_attempts: Comparative studies using bulk parameters such as average mixing enthalpy, atomic size difference, and valence electron concentration to predict phase formation have been made, but they typically fall short by not separately accounting for the role of local chemical ordering and short-range clustering effects in stabilizing specific phases.

decision.trend: Early research on Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys has focused on how compositional adjustments (notably varying Al content) and processing conditions such as annealing temperature lead to variations in phase structure. For example, one study showed that lower Al content tends to yield a single-phase disordered alloy resistant to irradiation‐induced precipitation, while higher Al levels promote multiphase behavior with ordered (B2) domains and associated nano-scale precipitates. Later work on eutectic AlCoCrFeNi alloys further revealed that controlled thermal aging can induce segregation and tempering-like embrittlement through the formation and evolution of ordered domains. These studies have successfully correlated processing parameters, precipitate morphology, and ordering, but they stop short of unifying these effects into a single mechanistic framework that explains how local chemical order governs phase stability across demanding service conditions.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress, it remains unresolved how the interplay between local chemical order (influenced by atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy) and the stability of ordered versus disordered phases governs the alloy’s multi-environment performance (high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness). In particular, the specific compositional and thermal boundaries where local ordering drives phase transformations—and how these changes directly link to mechanical and functional properties—remain unclear.
decision.lever: Systematically vary annealing temperature and time—while keeping the global composition constant—to control the degree of short-range chemical order (e.g., promoting or suppressing B2 ordering). The proposed experiment would compare a baseline Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy to alloys subjected to modified thermal treatments designed to enhance local chemical ordering, with key measurements being phase fraction shifts, transformation temperatures, and correlated changes in mechanical properties.
decision.why: This approach follows the observed trend where processing-induced ordering (as seen in previous studies) affects phase formation and performance. By isolating the effect of local chemical ordering via controlled thermal treatments, the experiment offers a clear, testable metric to directly link short-range order to phase stability. If the controlled change in annealing parameters leads to the predicted modification in phase fractions and property shifts, the hypothesis is supported; failure to observe these shifts would falsify the unified mechanistic explanation.
